transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what's been troubling you and what brings you in today?

Hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. I... I just don't really know what's happening to me lately, and honestly, I've been debating whether or not to even come in, but things have just gotten so strange. I'm a teaching assistant over at the university—I'm in a graduate program there—and normally I just love being on campus. I love the energy of the students and the history of the place, but recently... well, what scares me the absolute most, and the main reason I finally picked up the phone to make this appointment, is this bizarre feeling I keep getting. 

When I walk across campus now, say, from the library to my seminar room, it feels like... it's like I’m watching everything happen through a thick pane of glass. I know I'm walking, I know I'm moving my legs, but it feels like I’m not fully inside my own body. I'll look down at my hands carrying my grading folders and they just seem disconnected from me. And it's not just me, it's everything else, too. The brick buildings that I've walked past a thousand times, the undergrads rushing by on their phones or laughing... they all seem slightly unreal. Like they're part of a movie set or some strange dream that I just can't wake up from. I try to shake it off, I really do. I'll stop and try to focus on the trees or grab a coffee to ground myself, but the feeling just sticks to me. It's terrifying, honestly, because I need to be present and sharp for my students, but instead I just feel like I'm floating through this fake, distant version of the world.
Can you tell me if the feeling of being disconnected from yourself and the feeling that the world around you seems unreal happen at the same time, or do they feel like separate experiences to you?

Oh, wow, um... I've actually never tried to pick it apart like that. That's... it's really hard to say, honestly. Because when it hits me, it's just so incredibly overwhelming that I'm not really taking notes on what's happening first or if they're happening at the exact same second, you know? 

Like, just the other day, I was sitting at my desk—I share this tiny, cramped office with three other TAs in the basement of the humanities building, which is already kind of claustrophobic on a good day—and I was trying to grade these midterm essays. And I remember looking down at my red pen, and my fingers just looked... foreign. Like they belonged to a mannequin or something. But then, I don't know if it was at the exact same time, or maybe a second later, or maybe even before I noticed my hands, the whole office just started to feel like a cardboard box. Like a set piece in a play. 

So, I really don't know if it's a package deal where they hit me simultaneously, or if my brain just sort of cascades from one weird feeling into the next. It's all just this big, confusing blur of things not being right. I wish I could give you a better timeline or be more specific for you, but when you're trapped inside that weird little bubble, you're just trying so hard to act normal and hope nobody notices that you're completely disconnected. You're just trying to survive the moment. So... yeah, I really couldn't tell you if they're separate or not. It just all feels like one big, terrifying mess.

Can you tell me if these episodes of feeling detached from yourself and the world around you last for a continuous period of time, or if there are clear breaks where everything feels completely normal again in between them?

Gosh, um... you know, I’ve actually been trying to figure that out myself, and I just... I really don't have a clear answer for you. It’s so incredibly frustrating. Because, okay, let’s say it’s a Wednesday, right? I wake up, I make my coffee—I always do a pour-over, which takes a few minutes and usually requires me to be pretty focused—and during that time, I *think* I feel normal. I'm just a forty-two-year-old woman standing in my kitchen in my robe, watching the hot water drip. But then later, I try to analyze it, and I wonder, wait, was I actually feeling normal then, or was the fog just... maybe a little thinner in that exact moment? 

It's like, I can't tell if there are actual, solid breaks where that pane of glass completely shatters and I'm one hundred percent back in the real world, or if it's just this continuous, underlying hum of distance that just spikes up into those really terrifying episodes I told you about. Like, just the other afternoon, I was talking to the lead professor for my course about some syllabus changes we needed to make for the freshmen, and I was nodding and making eye contact, and I thought I was fully there. I felt engaged. But the absolute second I walked out of his office and shut the heavy wooden door, the hallway looked like a flat painting again. 

So did the feeling just come back right then? Or was it actually there the whole time we were talking, and I was just too distracted by trying to sound professional and keep my job to notice it? 

I really, really don't know. I tell my undergrads to be so precise with their citations and their timelines, and here I am, I can't even give you a definitive yes or no about my own brain. I wish I could say, 'Yes, it stops from 2 PM to 4 PM,' but I just haven't been able to track it like that. It’s exhausting, honestly, trying to monitor your own reality all day long while also trying to grade papers and lead discussions. So... yeah, I’m really not sure if there are clear breaks where I'm totally fine, or if it’s just one long, weird continuum that just gets louder and quieter.

Can you tell me if the feeling of being detached from yourself and the world comes and goes in distinct episodes, or if it feels more like a constant background experience that’s always there, even if it sometimes gets worse or less intense?

I know I sort of just touched on this, and I'm probably talking in circles, I'm sorry... it's just so hard to pin down. But if I really sit here and try to analyze it the way you're asking, I think... I think it has to be a constant background thing. 

Because, like I was trying to explain earlier, the thing that scares me the absolute most is that walk across campus. When I’m making that trek past the old clock tower and the student union, and I get that intense, horrible sensation that I’m watching everything through a thick pane of glass... that’s when it’s at its absolute peak. That’s when the feeling that I'm not fully inside my own body is so strong I can barely breathe, and all the undergrads and the brick buildings look so bizarrely unreal. 

But even when I’m not in the middle of a major, undeniable spike like that, I don't think the glass ever fully goes away. It’s like... you know when you leave a television on in the other room? You might not be actively watching it, you might even forget it's on while you're reading or doing dishes, but the low static hum is still there in the background, coloring the silence. That’s how this feels. So even when I'm just sitting in my apartment, trying to grade those essays, or just staring at my kitchen counter, there's this lingering, quiet sense that I'm just... slightly off. Slightly detached from myself. 

And then I'll have to go teach, and I'll step out onto the quad, and BAM, the volume turns all the way up. The students look like movie extras again, my legs don't feel like my legs, and I'm right back to watching my own life through that terrible window. So, yes, I think it's always there, humming in the background, just waiting to get worse. It’s exhausting, honestly, constantly wondering if I'm really here or if I'm just playing the part of a person who is here.

Have you ever had an episode where you suddenly felt detached from yourself or the world around you that only lasted for a few minutes or an hour and then went away completely, where everything felt totally back to normal afterward?

I... well, I feel like I kind of just answered that, but maybe I'm not explaining myself very well. I'm sorry, my brain is just so scattered lately. But to answer your question about it going away completely... no. I don't think so. 

Because, like I literally just mentioned, what scares me most is that when I walk across campus, it feels like I’m watching everything through glass. That specific, intense spike—where I feel like I’m not fully in my own body and the buildings and the students around me are slightly unreal—that part *does* only last for a few minutes. The walk from the humanities building to the library takes exactly fourteen minutes if I don't stop to talk to anyone. So that really severe episode, where I feel completely severed from myself and everything is just terrifyingly fake, that might only last for those fourteen minutes. Or maybe an hour, if the feeling lingers while I'm finding a desk and setting up my laptop in the stacks. 

But the thing is, when that peak ends... it doesn't go back to *totally* normal. It just doesn't. The glass might get a little thinner, and the students might start looking a little more like actual human beings instead of props, but I never feel completely anchored back in reality. I just go back to that low-level hum I was telling you about. I'll be sitting there in the library, looking at my research notes, and I'll think, "Okay, the worst of it is over," but my hands still feel just a tiny bit disconnected. The room still feels just a tiny bit hollow. 

So, no, I haven't had a time where it just completely vanished and I felt one hundred percent like myself again for the rest of the day. I really wish I did. I'd give anything for just an hour of actual, complete normalcy where I'm not constantly checking to see if I'm real. But it always just lingers.

Can you recall any specific time when the feelings of detachment or unreality started suddenly, lasted for a short time—like minutes or up to an hour—and then went away completely, where you felt entirely back to normal afterward?

Doctor, I... I feel like we’re just going in circles here, or maybe I’m really just doing a terrible job of explaining myself today. Which, honestly, is entirely possible given how backed up I am on grading these freshman midterms and how scattered my brain is. But... no. To be completely clear, no, it never goes away completely. 

Like I was just trying to say a minute ago, the absolute most terrifying part of all this—the thing that really scares me the most—is when I have to walk across campus. I'll step outside the humanities building, and suddenly it feels exactly like I’m watching everything through a thick pane of glass. It’s this incredibly intense rush where I feel like I’m not fully inside my own body anymore, and all the historic brick buildings and the undergrads rushing to class... they all just look slightly unreal. Like I've wandered onto a movie set and none of it has any actual depth. 

And yes, that really sharp, sudden, terrifying peak of it? That part might only last for the time it takes me to cross the quad, maybe ten or fifteen minutes, or up to an hour if the feeling follows me into the library. But the crucial thing—and I really want to make sure I'm making sense here—is that when that intense hour is over, I do not go back to normal. The glass doesn't shatter and disappear. It just gets a little thinner. I never, ever have a moment where the hour passes and I feel entirely, one hundred percent back to normal afterward. It always just settles back down into that constant, exhausting background hum I was telling you about. I would give absolutely anything for it to just stop completely, even for an afternoon, but it just doesn't work like that.

Can you think back to any time—maybe even before this started happening on campus—when you suddenly felt detached from yourself or the world, and then it completely went away afterward, leaving you feeling totally back to normal?

Doctor, I... I really don't mean to be difficult, I promise I don't, but I honestly feel like I'm losing my mind a little bit here. Are you... are you asking me the exact same question again? I know you added the part about before this started happening on campus, but... I just... I don't know how else to say it. No. Never. In my entire forty-two years of life, I have never experienced anything even remotely like this until recently. 

I know I keep bringing up that exact same example, and I'm sorry to keep beating a dead horse, but I keep going back to it because it is truly what terrifies me the absolute most out of everything. I never, ever used to feel like I was trapped behind a thick pane of glass. Before this semester, walking across the university was just... walking. I'd be thinking about my lesson plans, or wondering if I had enough coffee in my system to get through grading the rest of those freshman midterms. I was actually there. I was present. I never used to walk past the student union and feel like I wasn't actually inside my own skin. I never looked at the brick buildings or the undergrads walking by and felt like they were completely fake or slightly unreal. 

Before all this started, the world was just the world, and I was just me. So, no, I've never had a time in the past where this happened and then magically cleared up and I felt normal again. This whole feeling of being disconnected from myself and my surroundings... it is entirely new, and like I've been trying to explain, it just doesn't ever go away completely anymore. I really hope I'm answering what you're looking for this time, because I just don't know how else to explain that the glass is just always there now.
Can you recall if these feelings of detachment or unreality started around the same time as a particularly stressful or traumatic event in your life?

I mean... yes. Yes, it did. It started exactly then. I remember trying to go back to my normal schedule right after it happened, thinking that getting back into my routine as a TA would somehow help ground me. I figured, you know, I'm forty-two years old, I'm a graduate student, I have responsibilities, I should just be able to push through the stress of it and focus on my students. But that's exactly when this whole nightmare began. 

And I know I sound like a broken record today, and I'm so sorry I keep bringing up the exact same scenario, but it's just... it's because it really is the thing that scares me the most out of everything. That feeling I keep telling you about, where I'm walking across campus and it suddenly feels like I’m watching everything through a pane of glass? That started right after the event. I remember the very first time it hit me, right after everything happened. I was just trying to cross the quad to get to my department, and all of a sudden it was like I wasn't fully in my own body anymore. I was just sort of hovering, and all the buildings and the students around me just looked slightly unreal. Like they were just flat images or something. 

So, yes, to answer your question, that specific, terrifying detachment—the glass, the unreality of the campus, feeling like I'm not in my own skin—it all started right around that exact same time. It was never, ever like this before that happened.
